## 1. Where counts stop

[Module 1](01-text-as-data.qmd) built two count-based models: an n-gram language model and a TF-IDF classifier. Both treat each word as an atomic symbol, and both fail in the same two ways.

**Sparsity.** A trigram model estimates $P(w_t \mid w_{t-2}, w_{t-1})$ from the count $c(w_{t-2}, w_{t-1}, w_t)$. There are $|V|^3$ possible trigrams, where $V$ is the vocabulary and $|V|$ its size. With $|V| = 20{,}000$ that is $8 \times 10^{12}$ cells, and any corpus fills only a tiny fraction of them. Smoothing moves probability mass onto the empty cells, but it cannot tell a plausible unseen trigram from an absurd one.

**Words are unrelated symbols.** Both models represent a word $w$ as a *one-hot vector*: a vector in $\mathbb{R}^{|V|}$ with a 1 at the index of $w$ and 0 elsewhere. Any two different one-hot vectors are orthogonal, so their dot product is 0. To the model, *hotel* is exactly as far from *motel* as from *banana*. Two consequences:

- The n-gram model that has seen "the cat sat on the mat" learns nothing about "the dog sat on the rug". Every count is tied to exact word identities.
- The TF-IDF classifier learns one weight per word and class. A test document that says *striker* gets no help from the training documents that said *forward*.

What we want is a representation in which similar words have similar vectors, so that what the model learns about one word transfers to its neighbors. The representation should also be small: tens or hundreds of dimensions, not $|V|$.

## 2. The distributional hypothesis and dense vectors

**Distributional hypothesis.** Words that occur in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings (Harris, 1954; Firth, 1957: "You shall know a word by the company it keeps"). The *context* of a word occurrence is the set of words near it.

The hypothesis turns meaning, which we cannot observe, into co-occurrence statistics, which we can count. If *hotel* and *motel* are both found near *room*, *booked*, *night* and *cheap*, then a model that must predict those neighbors from the word alone is pushed to represent the two words alike.

**Embeddings.** We give each word $w \in V$ a dense vector $e_w \in \mathbb{R}^d$, its *embedding*, with dimension $d \ll |V|$ (typically 50 to 300). The vectors are the rows of an embedding matrix $E \in \mathbb{R}^{|V| \times d}$, and they are parameters: we learn them by gradient descent on a prediction task. Looking up $e_w$ is the same as multiplying the one-hot vector of $w$ by $E$, which is why an embedding layer is a linear layer with a one-hot input and no bias.

**Similarity** between two words is measured by the cosine of the angle between their embeddings:

$$
\cos(e_a, e_b) = \frac{e_a^\top e_b}{\lVert e_a \rVert \, \lVert e_b \rVert}
$$ {#eq-cosine}

where $\lVert \cdot \rVert$ is the Euclidean norm. Cosine ignores vector length, which tends to track word frequency rather than meaning. *Lab: Exercise 2 implements @eq-cosine to find nearest neighbors.*

## 3. Skip-gram with a full softmax

Word2vec's skip-gram model (Mikolov et al., 2013) turns the distributional hypothesis into a training objective: **given a word, predict the words around it.**

**Training pairs.** Take the corpus as one token sequence $w_1, \dots, w_T$. Choose a window half-width $m$ (for example $m = 2$). For each position $t$, the *center word* is $w_t$ and the *context words* are $w_{t+j}$ for $-m \le j \le m$, $j \ne 0$. Each (center, context) pair is one training example. We write a generic pair as $(w, o)$: center word $w$, context ("outside") word $o$.

![Skip-gram training pairs. With half-width $m = 2$, the center word $w_t$ (*fox*) is paired with each of the four words in its window, giving four (center, context) pairs $(w, o)$.](/images/02-skipgram-window.svg){#fig-skipgram-window fig-alt="A sentence of eight tokens with the center word fox highlighted and a window of two words on each side bracketed. Arrows run from fox to quick, brown, jumps and over. Beside the sentence, the four training pairs are listed: (fox, quick), (fox, brown), (fox, jumps), (fox, over)."}

**Two vectors per word.** Each word gets two embeddings:

- $e_w \in \mathbb{R}^d$, used when $w$ is the center word (row $w$ of $E$);
- $u_w \in \mathbb{R}^d$, used when $w$ is a context word (row $w$ of a second matrix $U \in \mathbb{R}^{|V| \times d}$).

The parameters are $\theta = \{E, U\}$. Two matrices keep the model simple: with a single matrix, the score of a word with itself, $e_w^\top e_w$, would be large, yet a word rarely appears in its own context. After training we keep $E$ as the word vectors and usually discard $U$.

**The model.** The score of a pair is the dot product $u_o^\top e_w$. A softmax over the vocabulary turns scores into a probability:

$$
P_\theta(o \mid w) = \frac{\exp(u_o^\top e_w)}{\sum_{v \in V} \exp(u_v^\top e_w)}
$$ {#eq-softmax}

**The loss** is the average negative log-likelihood of the observed context words:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{softmax}}(\theta) = -\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{\substack{-m \le j \le m \\ j \ne 0}} \log P_\theta(w_{t+j} \mid w_t)
$$ {#eq-sg-loss}

**Why this is too slow.** Take one pair $(w, o)$ and differentiate $-\log P_\theta(o \mid w)$ with respect to the center vector. Write $-\log P_\theta(o \mid w) = -u_o^\top e_w + \log \sum_{v} \exp(u_v^\top e_w)$. Then

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial e_w} \big( -\log P_\theta(o \mid w) \big)
= -u_o + \sum_{v \in V} \frac{\exp(u_v^\top e_w)}{\sum_{v'} \exp(u_{v'}^\top e_w)} \, u_v
= -u_o + \sum_{v \in V} P_\theta(v \mid w) \, u_v .
$$ {#eq-softmax-grad}

The gradient is "observed context vector minus expected context vector". The expectation is a sum over the whole vocabulary, so every training pair costs $O(|V|)$ and touches every row of $U$. With billions of pairs and $|V|$ in the hundreds of thousands, this is the bottleneck. *Lab: @eq-softmax and @eq-sg-loss are shown in a provided cell for a timing comparison; you do not implement them.*

## 4. Negative sampling

Negative sampling (Mikolov et al., 2013) replaces the $|V|$-way prediction with a much cheaper binary one. This is the derivation the lab implements, so we take it step by step.

**Step 1: change the question.** Instead of "which word is in the context of $w$?", ask "is the pair $(w, o)$ a real pair from the corpus, or a fake one?" Let $D \in \{0, 1\}$ be that label: $D = 1$ for a real pair. Model it with logistic regression on the same dot-product score:

$$
P_\theta(D = 1 \mid w, o) = \sigma(u_o^\top e_w), \qquad \sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}
$$ {#eq-binary}

where $\sigma$ is the sigmoid function.

**Step 2: make fake pairs.** A classifier needs negative examples. For each real pair $(w, o)$, draw $K$ *negative samples* $\tilde{w}_1, \dots, \tilde{w}_K$ from a *noise distribution* $P_n$ over the vocabulary and treat each $(w, \tilde{w}_k)$ as a fake pair. Mikolov et al. report that $K$ between 5 and 20 works for small corpora and 2 to 5 for large ones. For the noise distribution they found the unigram distribution raised to the power $3/4$ to work best:

$$
P_n(v) = \frac{c(v)^{3/4}}{\sum_{v' \in V} c(v')^{3/4}}
$$ {#eq-noise}

where $c(v)$ is the count of word $v$ in the corpus. The exponent flattens the distribution: rare words are drawn more often than their raw frequency, very frequent words less often. The value $3/4$ is empirical, not derived. *Lab: @eq-noise is the provided function `noise_distribution`.*

**Step 3: write the likelihood.** Treat the $K + 1$ labels as independent. The real pair should be classified $D = 1$ and each fake pair $D = 0$:

$$
\underbrace{\sigma(u_o^\top e_w)}_{\text{real pair is real}} \; \prod_{k=1}^{K} \underbrace{\big(1 - \sigma(u_{\tilde{w}_k}^\top e_w)\big)}_{\text{fake pair is fake}}
$$

**Step 4: simplify with $1 - \sigma(x) = \sigma(-x)$.** This identity follows from the definition: $1 - \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}} = \frac{e^{-x}}{1 + e^{-x}} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{x}} = \sigma(-x)$. Take the negative log of the likelihood to get the loss for one pair:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{SGNS}}(w, o) = -\log \sigma(u_o^\top e_w) \; - \sum_{k=1}^{K} \log \sigma(-u_{\tilde{w}_k}^\top e_w), \qquad \tilde{w}_k \sim P_n
$$ {#eq-sgns}

This is the skip-gram negative-sampling (SGNS) loss. The training loss is its average over all (center, context) pairs in the corpus. The first term pulls $e_w$ and $u_o$ together (large dot product); the second pushes $e_w$ away from the context vectors of random words. *Lab: Exercise 1 implements @eq-sgns as `sgns_loss`.*

![Negative sampling as binary classification. The real pair $(w, o)$ and $K = 3$ noise pairs $(w, \tilde{w}_k)$ each pass a dot-product score through a sigmoid. The target label is $D = 1$ for the real pair and $D = 0$ for the noise pairs.](/images/02-sgns-binary.svg){#fig-sgns-binary fig-alt="Four rows. The first row is the real pair (w, o): its score, u_o transpose e_w, feeds a sigmoid, and the target label is D = 1. The other three rows are noise pairs (w, w-tilde-1) to (w, w-tilde-3): each score, u_w-tilde-k transpose e_w, feeds a sigmoid, and the target label is D = 0."}

**Step 5: the gradients.** We need one derivative: $\frac{d}{dx} \log \sigma(x) = \frac{\sigma'(x)}{\sigma(x)} = 1 - \sigma(x)$, using $\sigma'(x) = \sigma(x)(1 - \sigma(x))$. Replacing $x$ by $-x$ and applying the chain rule gives $\frac{d}{dx} \log \sigma(-x) = -(1 - \sigma(-x)) = -\sigma(x)$. Apply the chain rule to each term of @eq-sgns:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{SGNS}}}{\partial e_w} &= -\big(1 - \sigma(u_o^\top e_w)\big)\, u_o \;+\; \sum_{k=1}^{K} \sigma(u_{\tilde{w}_k}^\top e_w)\, u_{\tilde{w}_k} \\[4pt]
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{SGNS}}}{\partial u_o} &= -\big(1 - \sigma(u_o^\top e_w)\big)\, e_w \\[4pt]
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{SGNS}}}{\partial u_{\tilde{w}_k}} &= \sigma(u_{\tilde{w}_k}^\top e_w)\, e_w
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-sgns-grad}

(If the same word is drawn twice among the negatives, its gradients add.) Read each line as "prediction error times the other vector": the error is $\sigma(\cdot) - D$, the predicted probability minus the label. It is the logistic-regression gradient from Module 1, with the difference that both the "features" and the "weights" are learned.

**What we gained.** One update now touches $K + 2$ vectors instead of $|V| + 1$: the cost per pair drops from $O(|V|)$ to $O(K)$. *Lab: the Exercise 1 checkpoint compares autograd's gradient of your `sgns_loss` against @eq-sgns-grad.*

**What we gave up.** @eq-sgns is not an approximation of the softmax likelihood @eq-sg-loss, and $\sigma(u_o^\top e_w)$ is not a normalized distribution over words. SGNS gives good vectors, not a language model.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Optional: subsampling frequent words"}
Words such as *the* appear in almost every window and say little about their neighbors. Mikolov et al. (2013) discard each occurrence of word $v$ before building pairs with probability

$$
P_{\text{discard}}(v) = 1 - \sqrt{\frac{\tau}{f(v)}}
$$

(taken as 0 when negative), where $f(v) = c(v) / T$ is the relative frequency of $v$ and $\tau$ is a threshold, typically around $10^{-5}$ for very large corpora. This speeds up training and improves the vectors of rare words. The lab applies it in the provided data pipeline with a larger $\tau$ suited to a small corpus.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Optional: what SGNS is really computing"}
Levy and Goldberg (2014) showed that, with enough dimensions, the SGNS optimum satisfies

$$
u_o^\top e_w = \mathrm{PMI}(w, o) - \log K, \qquad \mathrm{PMI}(w, o) = \log \frac{P(w, o)}{P(w)\,P(o)}
$$

where PMI is the pointwise mutual information of the pair, estimated from co-occurrence counts. So SGNS implicitly factorizes a shifted PMI matrix. This connects word2vec back to the count-based methods of Module 1: the neural model is a compact, weighted factorization of a count matrix, not a different kind of object.
:::

## 5. CBOW and GloVe in brief

**CBOW** (continuous bag of words) is skip-gram reversed. It averages the embeddings of the context words and predicts the center word from that average. It trains faster, because there is one prediction per window rather than $2m$; skip-gram tends to do better on rare words.

**GloVe** (Pennington et al., 2014) starts from global counts rather than a stream of windows. Let $c(w, o)$ be the number of times $o$ occurs in the context of $w$ over the whole corpus. GloVe fits the vectors by weighted least squares so that dot products match log counts:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{GloVe}} = \sum_{w, o \,:\, c(w,o) > 0} f\big(c(w, o)\big) \, \big( e_w^\top u_o + b_w + \tilde{b}_o - \log c(w, o) \big)^2
$$ {#eq-glove}

where $b_w$ and $\tilde{b}_o$ are per-word scalar biases and $f$ is a weighting function that grows as $(x / x_{\max})^{3/4}$ and is capped at 1 for $x \ge x_{\max}$, so that rare pairs count for less and very frequent pairs do not dominate. Skip-gram and GloVe use the same co-occurrence information and give vectors of similar quality. *Lab: the stretch section loads pretrained GloVe vectors; you do not train @eq-glove.*

**Analogies.** Trained embeddings show approximately linear structure: the offset $e_{\text{king}} - e_{\text{man}}$ is close to $e_{\text{queen}} - e_{\text{woman}}$. An analogy "$a$ is to $b$ as $a'$ is to ?" is answered by

$$
\arg\max_{v \in V \setminus \{a, b, a'\}} \cos\big(e_v, \; e_b - e_a + e_{a'}\big)
$$ {#eq-analogy}

Note the excluded set: without it the answer is usually one of the three input words. *Lab: @eq-analogy is the provided function `analogy`, which calls your Exercise 2 function.*

## 6. PyTorch refresher

Everything from here to Module 12 is written in PyTorch. Four ideas are enough for today.

1. **Tensors** are arrays that live on a device (CPU or GPU) and may record the operations applied to them.
2. **Autograd.** If a tensor has `requires_grad=True`, calling `.backward()` on a scalar computed from it fills in `.grad` with the derivative. We write the loss; PyTorch applies the chain rule.
3. **`nn.Module`** bundles parameters with a `forward` method. `nn.Embedding(V, d)` holds the matrix $E$ and returns rows of it; `nn.Linear(a, b)` holds a weight matrix and a bias.
4. **The training loop** is always the same five lines.

```python
import torch, torch.nn as nn

class SkipGram(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size, d):
        super().__init__()
        self.E = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d)   # center vectors  e_w
        self.U = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d)   # context vectors u_w

    def forward(self, center, context, negatives):
        # center, context: (B,)   negatives: (B, K)
        return sgns_loss(self.E(center), self.U(context), self.U(negatives))

model = SkipGram(vocab_size=20_000, d=100)
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

for center, context, negatives in loader:          # 1. get a batch
    loss = model(center, context, negatives)       # 2. forward pass: compute the loss
    opt.zero_grad()                                # 3. clear old gradients
    loss.backward()                                # 4. backward pass: autograd
    opt.step()                                     # 5. update the parameters
```

`B` is the batch size. The function `sgns_loss` is @eq-sgns averaged over the batch: the one piece you write in Exercise 1. Step 4 computes @eq-sgns-grad for you, and only for the rows of $E$ and $U$ that the batch used.

## 7. Feed-forward networks and backpropagation

Embeddings give us features. To use them for classification we need a model on top. Module 1's classifier was linear in its input; a feed-forward network adds one nonlinear layer.

**From words to a document vector.** A document is a token sequence $w_1, \dots, w_T$. The simplest fixed-size representation is the average of its word embeddings:

$$
x = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} e_{w_t} \; \in \mathbb{R}^d
$$ {#eq-avg}

This replaces Module 1's TF-IDF vector in $\mathbb{R}^{|V|}$ with a dense vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$. *Lab: Exercise 3 implements @eq-avg as `average_embeddings`.*

**The network.** With input $x$, label $y \in \{1, \dots, C\}$ and $C$ classes:

$$
\begin{aligned}
h &= \mathrm{ReLU}(W_1 x + b_1) && W_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h \times d},\; b_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h} \\
z &= W_2 h + b_2 && W_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times d_h},\; b_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{C} \\
\hat{y} &= \mathrm{softmax}(z) && \hat{y}_i = \frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{C} \exp(z_j)} \\
\mathcal{L} &= -\log \hat{y}_y
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ffn}

Here $h$ is the hidden vector with $d_h$ units, $\mathrm{ReLU}(a) = \max(0, a)$ applied elementwise, $z$ are the logits, $\hat{y}$ the predicted class probabilities and $\mathcal{L}$ the cross-entropy loss. Without the ReLU, the two layers would collapse into one linear map and we would be back at logistic regression. *Lab: Exercise 4 implements the forward pass of @eq-ffn as `FeedForwardClassifier.forward`.*

**Backpropagation** is the chain rule applied from the loss backwards, reusing each intermediate result. Let $\mathrm{onehot}(y) \in \mathbb{R}^C$ be the one-hot vector of the label, $a = W_1 x + b_1$ the hidden pre-activation, and $\delta$ denote the gradient of $\mathcal{L}$ with respect to a layer's pre-activation.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\delta_z &= \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z} = \hat{y} - \mathrm{onehot}(y) \\[2pt]
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W_2} &= \delta_z \, h^\top, \qquad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial b_2} = \delta_z \\[2pt]
\delta_a &= \big(W_2^\top \delta_z\big) \odot \mathbf{1}[a > 0] \\[2pt]
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W_1} &= \delta_a \, x^\top, \qquad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial b_1} = \delta_a
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-backprop}

where $\odot$ is the elementwise product and $\mathbf{1}[a > 0]$ is 1 where the hidden unit was active and 0 elsewhere (the derivative of ReLU). The first line comes from differentiating $\mathcal{L} = -z_y + \log \sum_j \exp(z_j)$: the derivative with respect to $z_i$ is $\hat{y}_i$, minus 1 when $i = y$. It has the same "prediction minus target" form as @eq-softmax-grad and @eq-sgns-grad. Each later line multiplies the error arriving from above by the local derivative of one layer. *Lab: you do not write @eq-backprop; `loss.backward()` computes it. A provided cell checks autograd's $\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial z$ against $\hat{y} - \mathrm{onehot}(y)$.*

One more step of the chain rule gives $\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial x = W_1^\top \delta_a$, and through @eq-avg a gradient for every embedding in the document. So embeddings can be trained by the classification loss too. In the lab's core path they stay frozen, so that the comparison with TF-IDF measures the features and nothing else.

## 8. Bengio's neural language model

We now have what is needed to repair the n-gram language model. Bengio et al. (2003) keep the n-gram assumption, that the next word depends on the previous $n - 1$ words, but replace the count table with a feed-forward network over embeddings.

Concatenate the embeddings of the $n - 1$ context words, pass them through one hidden layer, and take a softmax over the vocabulary:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= [\, e_{w_{t-n+1}} ; \dots ; e_{w_{t-1}} \,] \in \mathbb{R}^{(n-1)d} \\
h &= \tanh(W_1 x + b_1) \\
P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{t-n+1}, \dots, w_{t-1}) &= \mathrm{softmax}(W_2 h + b_2)_{w_t}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-nplm}

with $W_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h \times (n-1)d}$ and $W_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{|V| \times d_h}$. The loss is the average negative log-likelihood of the next word, and its exponential is the perplexity from Module 1, $\mathrm{PPL} = \exp\big(-\tfrac{1}{T} \sum_t \log P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t})\big)$, so the two kinds of model can be compared directly.

![Bengio's neural language model with $n - 1 = 3$ context words. Every position looks up its word in the same embedding matrix $E$. The three embeddings are concatenated into $x$, a tanh hidden layer gives $h$, and a softmax over $|V|$ gives the next-word distribution.](/images/02-bengio-nplm.svg){#fig-bengio-nplm fig-alt="Left to right: three context words, w_{t-3}, w_{t-2} and w_{t-1}, are each looked up in the same shared embedding matrix E. The three embeddings are concatenated into one vector x, which passes through weights W_1 and a tanh hidden layer h, then through weights W_2 and a softmax, giving a bar chart of the next-word distribution over the vocabulary."}

This addresses both failures from Part 1:

- **Sparsity.** The parameter count is $|V| d + d_h (n-1) d + |V| d_h$ plus biases: linear in $|V|$ and in $n$, where the n-gram table has $|V|^n$ cells.
- **Unrelated symbols.** If *cat* and *dog* have similar embeddings, a context containing *dog* produces nearly the same $x$, hence nearly the same prediction, as one containing *cat*. Probability mass reaches unseen n-grams through similarity, not through a smoothing constant.

The embeddings here are learned by the language-modeling loss itself. Word2vec, ten years later, kept the embedding table and removed the hidden layer and the full softmax to make training on billions of words practical. *Lab: @eq-nplm is not implemented in Lab 2. Module 3's lab trains a neural language model and compares its perplexity with the n-gram baseline.*

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Optional: details of the original model"}
The model in Bengio et al. (2003) also has optional direct connections from $x$ to the output layer, omitted in @eq-nplm. Its output softmax has the same $O(|V|)$ cost per example as @eq-softmax; that cost is what later work, including hierarchical softmax and negative sampling, set out to reduce.
:::

**What is still missing.** Both models in this module use a fixed, small amount of context, and neither handles word order well:

- Averaging (@eq-avg) is a bag of words. "The dog bit the man" and "the man bit the dog" get the same vector.
- The neural language model sees exactly $n - 1$ words. A dependency longer than the window is invisible, and widening the window grows $W_1$ and gives every position its own separate weights.
- Each word has one vector regardless of context: *bank* is the same in "river bank" and "bank account".

[Module 3](03-sequence-models.qmd) takes up the first two: recurrent networks read a sequence of any length in order, carrying a hidden state $h_t$ from one token to the next. The third waits for contextual representations in Modules 5 and 6.

## Summary

- Count-based models fail on sparsity and on treating words as unrelated symbols. Dense embeddings $e_w \in \mathbb{R}^d$ address both.
- The distributional hypothesis supplies the training signal: predict a word's neighbors.
- Skip-gram with a full softmax costs $O(|V|)$ per pair. Negative sampling replaces it with $K + 1$ binary classifications, giving the loss @eq-sgns at cost $O(K)$.
- Every gradient in this module has the form "prediction minus target, times the other side's vector".
- A feed-forward network over averaged embeddings is a dense replacement for TF-IDF plus a linear classifier. Whether it is more accurate is an empirical question that the lab measures on the same test split.
- Bengio's neural language model applies the same pieces to next-word prediction and generalizes to unseen n-grams through embedding similarity.
- Open problem for Module 3: order and long-range dependence.

## Common misconceptions

1. **"Negative sampling is a fast approximation of the softmax."** It is a different objective. It does not yield normalized probabilities $P_\theta(o \mid w)$ and cannot be used to compute perplexity.
2. **"Similar vectors mean synonyms."** Cosine similarity reflects shared contexts. Antonyms (*hot*, *cold*) and co-hyponyms (*Tuesday*, *Friday*) share contexts and end up close.
3. **"The analogy trick shows the model understands relations."** The result depends on excluding the input words in @eq-analogy and on the corpus. On a small corpus most analogies fail; the lab shows this.
4. **"An embedding layer is a special kind of layer."** It is a linear layer applied to a one-hot vector, implemented as a row lookup.
5. **"Dense embeddings must beat TF-IDF."** Averaging discards word order and blurs distinctive words. On topic classification with plenty of labeled data, TF-IDF with a linear model is a strong baseline. Measure before claiming.
6. **"Each word has one meaning, so one vector is enough."** Static embeddings merge all senses of a word into one point. That limitation motivates the contextual models of Day 2.

## Readings

1. Mikolov, T., Sutskever, I., Chen, K., Corrado, G. and Dean, J. (2013). [Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.4546). *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 26*. The negative-sampling paper: sections 2.2 and 2.3.
2. Goldberg, Y. and Levy, O. (2014). [word2vec Explained: deriving Mikolov et al.'s negative-sampling word-embedding method](https://arxiv.org/abs/1402.3722). arXiv:1402.3722. A slower version of the derivation in Part 4.
3. Pennington, J., Socher, R. and Manning, C. (2014). [GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation](https://aclanthology.org/D14-1162/). *EMNLP 2014*, pages 1532–1543.
4. Bengio, Y., Ducharme, R., Vincent, P. and Jauvin, C. (2003). [A Neural Probabilistic Language Model](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v3/bengio03a.html). *Journal of Machine Learning Research* 3, pages 1137–1155.
5. Jurafsky, D. and Martin, J. H. [*Speech and Language Processing*](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/) (3rd edition draft), the chapters "Embeddings" and "Neural Networks". Chapter numbers change between drafts; go by title.

Also cited above: Mikolov, T., Chen, K., Corrado, G. and Dean, J. (2013). [Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.3781). arXiv:1301.3781 (skip-gram and CBOW). Levy, O. and Goldberg, Y. (2014). [Neural Word Embedding as Implicit Matrix Factorization](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2014/hash/b78666971ceae55a8e87efb7cbfd9ad4-Abstract.html). *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 27*. Harris, Z. (1954). Distributional Structure. *Word* 10(2–3). Firth, J. R. (1957). A Synopsis of Linguistic Theory, 1930–1955. In *Studies in Linguistic Analysis*.
